bodyHtml:
Tomato prices climbed 31% year-on-year in India through mid-2026, and edible oil and LPG moved a further 10% on top of that — which is exactly why restaurants that used to recost a dish once a year are now doing it monthly. That's the right move for protecting margin. It also quietly exposes a gap in one of the most common free tools a restaurant picks up early: a QR code that has the entire menu packed inside the code itself. Every time a price changes, the code changes with it — and every printed copy of that code, on every table, counter and delivery bag, is now showing the wrong price until someone reprints it.

Why a free QR menu breaks the moment a price moves

Setu's free QR Menu Generator works by compressing the whole menu — categories, dishes, prices, veg/non-veg tags — directly into the QR code image, with no hosting, no signup and nothing stored on a server. That's genuinely useful: there's no subscription, no link that can ever go dead, and the menu lives entirely in the restaurant's own browser. The tradeoff is structural rather than a bug — because the menu is the code, editing so much as one price produces a different QR code. The sticker on table 4 and the one taped to the counter don't update themselves.

The ceiling most restaurants don't see coming

There's a second limit that shows up as menus grow: the whole menu has to fit inside roughly 2,900 characters, which works out to somewhere between 60 and 100 dishes depending on how much description text each item carries. A short QSR menu never notices. A full-service restaurant with sizes, variations and descriptive copy on every dish can hit that ceiling faster than expected — and the fix, again, is a new code and a fresh reprint.

Why 2026's price volatility makes this bite harder

None of this mattered much when a menu got priced once at launch and left alone for a year. In 2026, with ingredient costs this volatile, that's no longer how a well-run kitchen operates — recipe costing has become a monthly discipline for anyone tracking tomato, edible oil and LPG closely, and pricing follows the recosting. The more often a restaurant recosts and reprices — which is exactly the right habit this year — the more often a menu built on a self-contained QR code needs every physical copy replaced. A free tool that costs nothing to use can still cost real time and reprinting effort every single time the numbers move.

What a permanent-link QR code changes

The premium QR Menu flips the structure around: the printed code holds a short, permanent link, and the actual menu lives online where it can be edited any time. Change a price at 11pm and the table tents printed months ago are already showing it correctly — nothing to reprint, no new code to generate. That structural change also removes the size ceiling entirely, since the code only ever needs to carry a link, not the menu itself, which opens up dish photos, sold-out toggles, size and variation options, multiple menus (lunch, dinner, a seasonal card) that can be swapped without touching the printed code, and daily scan counts to see whether the table tents are actually getting used.

A simple way to know which one you need

The free tool is still the right starting point for most restaurants, and Setu keeps it free with no catch — not a trial, not a lead-in with a countdown. The signal to move up isn't the tool being free or paid, it's how often reprinting is actually happening. A menu that hasn't changed in months has no reason to switch. A menu getting repriced monthly because of ingredient swings, or one that's outgrown the 60–100 dish range, or one where photos and sold-out toggles would genuinely help conversion, is exactly the case the permanent-link version was built for.

Moving up doesn't mean starting over

Restaurants already using the free QR Menu Generator don't lose that work when they upgrade — pasting the free tool's menu link into the premium editor carries across the dishes, tagline, phone number, address and brand colour already set up, so switching is a five-minute step rather than a rebuild. And every restaurant that signs up gets the premium version free for a full 12 months, every feature included, no card required. After that first year it settles at ₹49 a month or ₹499 a year in India (roughly two months free on the annual plan), or $0.99 a month or $9.99 a year outside India.

Where this fits with the rest of your menu discipline

A QR code is only as accurate as the price behind it, and getting that price right in the first place is the harder half of this problem — which is exactly what recosting a dish properly in 2026 is about. Once the numbers are right, the QR code should be the last thing standing between a price change and a customer seeing it correctly — not a reason to put off a reprice you know you need to make.
